title: The frontier fort (312–319)
hookLine: guard yourself like a border town, guarded within and without

lines: THE WEAK GATE, THE SLEEPY GUARD.
cards: A capital city has big armies and thick walls. A town on the frontier has neither. It sits at the edge, where trouble arrives first, and its people can't afford to be casual.
They know which gate is weak, which stretch of wall is crumbling, which night the guards get sleepy. They check them all, every day, and inside the walls they keep order too.
Today's verse takes a town like that as a picture of a person.

teach.h: DO IT WITH YOUR WHOLE STRENGTH.
teach.b: The downward course keeps going with plain advice. A slack effort, a vow half kept, a doubtful discipline: none of these brings much fruit. If something is worth doing, do it with your whole strength.
A bad deed is better left undone, one verse says, because it burns you afterward; a good deed is better done, because it doesn't.

teach.h: A FORT GUARDED WITHIN AND WITHOUT.
teach.b: Then verse three hundred fifteen, in Max Müller's English: "Like a well-guarded frontier fort, with defences within and without, so let a man guard himself." Within and without.

The walls face outward, against what comes in through the senses: the ad, the insult, the easy temptation. But the fort also keeps watch inside, over the moods and thoughts that start their own trouble.
Let no moment slip past, the verse goes on: those who let the right moment pass suffer for it later, in the downward course. The chapter's last verses are a surprise.

teach.h: SHAME AND FEAR AT THE WRONG TARGET.
teach.b: They're about shame and fear aimed at the wrong target. Some people are ashamed of what isn't shameful, and not of what is. Some fear what isn't dangerous, and shrug at what is.
They see wrong where there is none, and miss it where it is. So guarding the fort isn't being anxious about everything.
A good guard knows which gate is actually weak.
Buddhist teaching calls this guarding indriya-saṃvara, restraint of the senses: keeping watch at the doors of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind. It isn't a wall to hide behind.
It's attention, placed where it's needed.

how: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners train in guarding the sense doors, noticing what comes in through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind; teachers often use the frontier-fort verse to describe it.

o: a soldier's lonely post at the edge of a kingdom
a person guarded within and without, like a border town
a wall you build to shut the world out for good

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.

s: the fort only guards against things outside
the verse says within and without: the senses and the mind.
the chapter warns against fearing the wrong things
some fear what isn't dangerous and shrug at what is.
guarding the fort means being anxious about everything
a good guard knows which gate is actually weak.

games.q: you're the guard of a small frontier town. you can watch every gate a little, or learn which gate trouble really uses. what do today's verses point toward?
o: watch every gate in a panic.
know the weak gate, and guard within and without.
stay inside and never open a gate.
games.why: the verses warn against fear aimed at the wrong target; the fort is guarded within and without, with attention where it's needed.

practice: Walk the walls of your own town and ask where trouble usually gets in: a gate on the outside, like a certain app, a certain conversation, a certain time of night, or a gate on the inside, like a mood that turns sour or a thought that loops.
Pick just one weak spot. Picture a calm guard standing there, not angry, just awake, and rest in the breath.

wordCard.voice: The frontier fort. A border town guarded within and without: watch the gates of the senses, and the mind inside.

carryVoice: Your line: guard the border town. Within and without, with a calm guard at the gate. See you tomorrow.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
sources.q: Like a well-guarded frontier fort, with defences within and without, so let a man guard himself.
